question: A program must keep the names of the players who join a game, and nobody knows in advance how many will join. What does an ArrayList offer here that a plain array does not?
correct: It grows and shrinks as elements are added and removed
incorrect: It stores primitives such as int directly, with no boxing
It reads the element at a given index faster than an array
It checks index bounds, while an array reads past its end
feedback: An array's length is fixed when it is created; an ArrayList resizes itself as you add and remove. The other three are real confusions. An ArrayList cannot hold primitives at all: a list of whole numbers is a List<Integer>, and each int is boxed. Indexed reads are, if anything, slightly faster on a plain array. And Java arrays DO check bounds: a bad index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, it does not read stray memory.

question:
Complete the declaration of a list that will hold int values such as 3 and 42:
List<___> nums = new ArrayList<>();
feedback: The type between the angle brackets must be a class, never a primitive, so List<int> does not compile. Integer is the wrapper class for int, and autoboxing converts between the two for you: nums.add(3) just works. The capital letter matters: integer and Int are not Java types.

question: A List<String> named words already exists. Write the statement that appends the String "Java" to the end of it.
feedback: add(element) appends to the end of the list, which then grows by one. (Since Java 21, addLast does the same job.) There is no words[...] = ... form: square brackets belong to arrays, and a list is changed only through its methods.

question: Arrange these lines into a working fragment that stores one name in a list and then prints how many letters that name has.
feedback: Each line needs the one before it. The list must exist before add can be called on it; get(0) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException on a list that is still empty; and first must hold a String before its length() can be read. The fragment prints 3.

question: words is a List<String> holding several words. Which statement copies the word at index 0 into first and leaves the list exactly as it was?
incorrect: String first = words[0];
String first = words.remove(0);
String first = words.get(1);
feedback: get(0) reads the element and changes nothing. words[0] is array syntax and does not compile for a list. remove(0) also hands back the element at index 0, but it deletes it from the list on the way out. get(1) reads the SECOND element, because list indexes start at 0 just as array indexes do. Since Java 21, words.getFirst() is another way to say get(0).

question: Java asks "how many?" in three different ways. An array answers with its {{1}} field (no parentheses), a String answers with its {{2}}() method, and an ArrayList answers with its {{3}}() method.
feedback: arr.length is a field, text.length() is a method, and list.size() is a method with a different name again. Mixing them up is a compile error, not a subtle bug: a list has no length and an array has no size().

question: One element is added in the middle of a list. What does this print?
feedback: add(1, "x") INSERTS at index 1: it overwrites nothing. Everything from index 1 onward shifts one place right, so the list becomes [a, x, b, c] and index 2 now holds b. If the line had been runes.set(1, "x"), b would have been replaced and index 2 would hold c.

question: Every time, the list starts as  t = [a, b, c]  (a List<String>). One statement runs, then t is printed. Match each statement to what is printed.
feedback: add(e) appends, and a list is happy to hold a second b. add(1, e) inserts and shifts the rest right, so the list grows. set(1, e) replaces, so the size stays at 3. remove(1) deletes whatever sits at index 1; remove("a") searches for the first element equal to "a" and deletes that.

question: A List<String> named log starts empty. The program calls log.add(...) {{a}} times, then log.remove(0) {{r}} times, then log.add(0, "start") once. What does log.size() return now?
feedback_template: Each add makes the list one longer, whether it appends or inserts at index 0. Each remove(0) makes it one shorter. So the size is {{a}} - {{r}} + 1 = {{expected}}. Inserting at index 0 shifts the other elements along; it does not overwrite one.

question: This fragment reads both ends of a list. What does it print?
feedback: size() is 4, so the last valid index is 3 and get(3) is 40. getFirst() (Java 21 and later) is get(0), which is 10; there is a matching getLast() too. Both values are int, so + adds them: 50. Asking for hp.get(hp.size()) would throw IndexOutOfBoundsException, exactly as arr[arr.length] does for an array.

question: names is a List<String>. Which of these visit every element of names, one at a time, without an error?
correct: for (int i = 0; i < names.size(); i++) { System.out.println(names.get(i)); }
incorrect: for (int i = 0; i < names.size(); i++) { System.out.println(names[i]); }
for (int i = 0; i <= names.size(); i++) { System.out.println(names.get(i)); }
feedback: The for-each loop, the index loop with get(i), and the forEach method all work. forEach takes a small piece of code written with an arrow: n -> ... means "given an element n, do this". names[i] is array syntax and does not compile for a list. The loop that uses <= runs one step too far: its last pass calls get(size()), which throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

correct: The compiler rejects words.add(42), so the program never runs
incorrect: It runs, and 42 is converted into the String "42" as it is stored
It compiles, then throws ClassCastException when the add runs
It runs, because the empty <> leaves the element type open
feedback: List<String> is a promise the compiler enforces: only Strings go in, so words.add(42) is a compile-time error and no exception is ever involved. Nothing converts 42 to "42" for you. The empty diamond <> does not leave the type open; it tells the compiler to copy the type from the left-hand side, so new ArrayList<>() here means new ArrayList<String>().

correct: The code that uses names relies on List alone, so a different list class can be swapped in by editing one word
incorrect: The variable becomes read-only, which protects the elements from being changed by accident
A List variable may hold elements of several types, while an ArrayList variable may not
List is the lighter type, so every call to get and add runs faster through it
feedback: List is an interface: a named set of methods (add, get, size, remove...) that every kind of list promises to have. ArrayList and LinkedList are two classes that keep that promise in different ways. If the variable's type is List, the rest of the code can use only those shared methods, so changing new ArrayList<>() to new LinkedList<>() is the only edit needed. The declared type does not make the list read-only, does not loosen the element type, and does not change the speed: the object is an ArrayList either way.

question: NPC: Index or value?
intro: Zoya lines up three numbered clay tokens on the bench: 5, 1, 9. "One method name, two different jobs," they say. "Java picks the job by looking at the TYPE of what you hand it."

beats.say: Here are my tokens as a list of Integer objects.
A list has two remove methods. remove(int index) deletes whatever sits at that position. remove(Object o) searches for an element equal to o and deletes that.
Now I write this. The 1 is a plain int.
An int matches remove(int index) exactly, so Java treats the 1 as a POSITION. It will not box the 1 into an Integer when an exact match is already on offer.

check.prompt: tokens was [5, 1, 9]. What is it after tokens.remove(1)?
check.why: Index 1 holds the value 1 here, so that element goes. It is a coincidence of my tokens: remove(1) means position 1.

beats.say: To remove BY VALUE from a list of numbers, hand over an Integer object instead of an int.
Integer.valueOf(9) is an object, so Java chooses remove(Object) and hunts for the element equal to 9. With a List<String> the trap never appears: a String can never be mistaken for an index.

outro: "Your turn. When you see remove with a number inside, ask: is that an int or an Integer? Then count positions from zero."

question: The list holds numbers, and the argument to remove is a number too. What does this print?
feedback: The argument 2 is an int, so Java chooses remove(int index) and deletes the element at POSITION 2, which is 30. The value 2 at the end of the list is untouched. To delete the value 2 instead you would write nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(2)), which selects remove(Object) and leaves [10, 20, 30].

question: indexOf searches a list from the front. What does this print?
code:
List<String> loot = new ArrayList<>(List.of("gem", "axe", "gem"));
System.out.println(loot.indexOf("gem") + " " + loot.indexOf("bow"));
feedback: indexOf returns the position of the FIRST element equal to its argument, so "gem" gives 0 even though there is another at index 2. When nothing matches it returns -1, a number that can never be a real index. It does not return null (the result is an int) and it does not throw. The + " " + in the middle makes this String concatenation, not arithmetic.

prompt: remove has two forms, and they hand back different things. Fill in what each line prints.
feedback: remove(int index) returns the element it took out, so the first call prints a. remove(Object) returns a boolean: true if it found and deleted a match ("c"), false if there was nothing to delete ("z"). A failed remove(Object) is not an error and throws nothing. Two elements are gone, so [b] is left.

incorrect: It does not compile, since List.of has no add method
It runs, and days then holds three elements
It runs, but the add is ignored and the size stays 2
feedback: List.of builds an IMMUTABLE list: its contents can never change. The variable's type is still List, and List has an add method, so the compiler is satisfied. The refusal comes at run time, as an UnsupportedOperationException, and it is loud rather than silent. set, remove and sort are refused the same way. Set.of and Map.of behave alike.

question: A fixed list is copied into an ArrayList. What does this print?
feedback: new ArrayList<>(fixed) makes a separate, changeable list that starts with the same three elements. Two adds and one remove leave the copy with 4; the original List.of list still has 3 and never noticed. This is the standard idiom when you want List.of's short syntax but need a list you can change.

question:
nums is an ArrayList<Integer> holding 3, 1, 2. What does this statement do?
nums.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder());
correct: It rearranges nums itself into 1, 2, 3 and returns nothing
incorrect: It returns a new list 1, 2, 3 and leaves nums as 3, 1, 2
It rearranges nums itself into 3, 2, 1, largest first
It fails to compile, as sort accepts Strings but not numbers
feedback: sort works IN PLACE: the list you call it on is rearranged, and the method's return type is void, so there is nothing to assign. Natural order means ascending for numbers and alphabetical for Strings, and both work. Largest-first needs Comparator.reverseOrder(). The older spelling Collections.sort(nums) does exactly the same job; it simply calls nums.sort for you.

question: Every time, nums starts as the ArrayList [3, 1, 2]. Match each fragment to what it prints.
feedback: The trap is reverse versus reverseOrder. Collections.reverse flips the list end to end without sorting anything, so [3, 1, 2] becomes [2, 1, 3]. Sorting with Comparator.reverseOrder() puts the largest first: [3, 2, 1]. max returns the largest element (3), frequency counts how many elements equal 3 (one), and indexOf says where 3 sits (position 0). The last three only look; they change nothing.

question: NPC: Who goes first?
intro: Zoya drops three name-tags on the bench: "pear", "fig", "apple". "Sorting needs a rule," they say. "In Java the rule is an object called a Comparator. Its whole job is to answer one question about two elements: which goes first?"

beats.say: sort takes the Comparator as its argument. The simplest rule is natural order: alphabetical for Strings, ascending for numbers.
Comparator.reverseOrder() is the same rule run backwards, so it would give [pear, fig, apple].
You can also build a rule from one property of each element. This one compares the tags by their length.
Read String::length as "for each String, use its length()". Shortest goes first, because lengths are numbers and numbers sort ascending.

check.prompt: After sorting [apple, fig, pear] by length, what does tags.getFirst() return?
check.why: fig has 3 letters, pear has 4 and apple has 5, so the order by length is [fig, pear, apple] and the first element is fig.

steps.say: Same list, three different orders, and the only thing I changed was the Comparator. The list does the sorting; the Comparator only supplies the rule.

beats.say: Same list, three different orders, and the only thing I changed was the Comparator. The list does the sorting; the Comparator only supplies the rule.

outro: "A monster ahead has sorted some words of its own. Work out its rule before you work out its answer."

question: The same list is sorted twice, by two different rules. What does this print?
feedback: reverseOrder() is alphabetical order backwards, so the list becomes [wolf, ox, hydra, bat] and a is wolf. Comparator.comparing(String::length) then orders by length, shortest first: ox has 2 letters, so b is ox. Each sort rearranges the same list in place; a and b were read at different moments.

question: The same five values go into a List and into a Set. What does this print?
feedback: A List keeps every element it is given, duplicates included, so its size is 5. A Set holds each distinct value once: the second and third "a" are quietly refused (add returns false, nothing is thrown), leaving a, b and c. That one difference is the usual reason to choose a Set.

feedback_template: The loop calls add {{n}} times, but a Set keeps each distinct value once. Integer division drops the remainder, so i / {{d}} gives 0 for the first {{d}} values of i, then 1 for the next {{d}}, and so on. The largest value added is the last i divided by {{d}}, and counting up from 0 to that value gives {{expected}} distinct numbers.

question: seen is a HashSet<String> that already holds "orc" and "elf". Which of these statements about it are true?
correct: seen.add("orc") returns false and leaves the set as it was
seen.contains("elf") stays quick even if the set grows to a million elements
incorrect: seen.add("orc") throws IllegalArgumentException, since duplicates are banned
seen.get(0) returns "orc", the element that was added first
A for-each loop over seen is sure to visit "orc" before "elf"
feedback: A duplicate add is refused politely: add returns false and nothing is thrown. (Set.of("orc", "orc") is the call that throws, not HashSet.add.) contains is fast because a HashSet jumps almost straight to where an element would be, using its hash code, instead of checking every element the way a list must. The price is that a HashSet has no positions: there is no get(index) at all, and the order a for-each loop visits the elements in is not the order they were added and is not promised to be anything in particular.

question: scores is a Map<String, Integer>. To store the pair "Ana" and 90 in it, you call scores.___("Ana", 90);
feedback: A map stores key-value pairs, and put(key, value) is how a pair goes in. Maps have no add method: add takes one element, and a map entry always has two parts. get(key) is how the value comes back out.

question: One key is put twice, and one key is never put at all. What does this print?
feedback: A map holds each key once. The second put for "orc" does not add an entry; it replaces the value 5 with 9, so there are 2 entries. get on a key that is absent returns null. It does not throw, and it does not return 0 even though the values are Integers.

feedback_template: size() counts distinct KEYS, not put calls. The keys are i % {{k}}, which can only be the remainders 0 up to one less than {{k}}. If the loop is long enough to wrap round, later puts land on keys that already exist and just replace their values; if it is not, every i is its own key. With {{n}} passes and a divisor of {{k}}, that leaves {{expected}} keys.

question:
stock is a Map<String, Integer> that has no entry for "axe". What happens at this line?
int n = stock.get("axe");
incorrect: n becomes 0, the default for a missing Integer
It throws NoSuchElementException
It does not compile: get returns an Integer, and n is an int
feedback: get returns null for a missing key. Assigning that to an int makes Java unbox it, and unboxing null throws NullPointerException. The line compiles happily, because Integer-to-int is normally automatic. There is no default of 0 for a missing key, and get never throws just because the key is absent. The safe spelling is stock.getOrDefault("axe", 0).

question: NPC: Counting with a map
intro: Zoya empties a sack of coloured beads onto the bench. "I want to know how many of each colour. A Map<String, Integer> is made for this: each colour is a key, and its value is the count so far."

beats.say: The whole trick is one line, run once for every bead.
getOrDefault(c, 0) means: give me the value stored for key c, or 0 if c is not a key yet. A plain get would hand back null for a new colour, and null + 1 crashes.

steps.say:
My beads are red, blue, red. First bead: red is not a key, so getOrDefault gives 0, and I put red with 1.
Second bead: blue is new as well, so blue goes in with 1. The map now has two entries.
Third bead: red again. This time getOrDefault finds the 1 that is already stored.

beats.say: My beads are red, blue, red. First bead: red is not a key, so getOrDefault gives 0, and I put red with 1.
Second bead: blue is new as well, so blue goes in with 1. The map now has two entries.
Third bead: red again. This time getOrDefault finds the 1 that is already stored.

check.prompt: What does the map hold after the third bead?
check.why: put on a key that already exists replaces its value, so red goes from 1 to 2. A map never holds the same key twice.

steps.say: So after the loop, counts.size() is the number of DIFFERENT colours, and counts.get("red") is how many red beads there were.

beats.say: So after the loop, counts.size() is the number of DIFFERENT colours, and counts.get("red") is how many red beads there were.

outro: "The next monster counts creatures instead of beads. Walk its list one word at a time, exactly as I did."

question: This is the counting idiom at work. What does it print?
feedback: Each pass looks up the count so far (0 for a creature not met before), adds 1, and puts it back under the same key. "elf" appears three times, so its value climbs 1, 2, 3. size() counts distinct keys: elf, orc, imp and bat make 4, however many times each was seen.

feedback_template: "axe" is already a key, so getOrDefault returns its stored {{a}}, and the put replaces that with {{a}} + {{b}}. "bow" is not a key yet, so getOrDefault falls back to 0 and "bow" goes in with 0 + {{c}}. Adding the two stored values gives {{expected}}. The 0 is used only when the key is missing.

question: m is a Map<String, Integer> holding exactly two entries: "a" with 1 and "b" with 2. Each expression is evaluated on that fresh map. Match each expression to the value it produces.
feedback: get gives null for an absent key, and getOrDefault gives your fallback instead. containsKey looks among the keys ("b" is one); containsValue looks among the values (1 and 2, so 3 is not there). remove(key) deletes the entry and hands back the value it held, here 1. values() is the collection of all the values, one per entry, so its size is 2.

prompt: ages is a Map<String, Integer>. Both loops add up everyone's age. Fill in the three method names.
feedback: A map cannot go straight into a for-each loop; you loop over one of its views. keySet() is the Set of keys, and inside the loop get(name) fetches each key's value. values() skips the keys and hands you the values directly, which is all a total needs. (entrySet() gives key and value together when you want both.)

question: NPC: Pulling bricks from a wall you are walking along
intro: Zoya writes a row of numbers on the slate: 4, -1, 7, -3, 8. "I want the negatives gone. Watch the obvious way fail first."

beats.say: The obvious way: walk the list with a for-each loop and remove the bad ones as I meet them.
A for-each loop keeps a bookmark in the list. Removing an element changes the list's SIZE behind the bookmark's back. On its next step the loop notices and throws ConcurrentModificationException.

steps.say:
Adding or removing is called a STRUCTURAL change, because it changes how many elements there are. That is what the loop objects to.
Replacing an element with set, or just reading, changes no sizes, so those are fine inside a for-each.

beats.say: Adding or removing is called a STRUCTURAL change, because it changes how many elements there are. That is what the loop objects to.
Replacing an element with set, or just reading, changes no sizes, so those are fine inside a for-each.

check.prompt: Which line is safe inside  for (int n : nums) { ... } ?
check.why: set swaps one element for another and the size stays the same. add and remove are structural changes.

beats.say: The right tool does the walking AND the removing for you:
Read the arrow as a test: "given an element n, is n < 0?" removeIf deletes every element whose answer is true.

outro: "Two monsters ahead: one tries the obvious way, one uses removeIf with a different test. You know how each story ends."

incorrect: It prints [rope, map, key]
It prints [rope, map, rock, key]
It does not compile: remove is not allowed in a for-each
feedback: Removing "rock" is a structural change: the list gets shorter while the for-each loop is part-way through it. When the loop asks for its next element it sees that the list changed underneath it and throws ConcurrentModificationException, so the println is never reached. The compiler cannot see this coming; the code is perfectly legal Java. bag.removeIf(item -> item.equals("rock")) does the job safely and leaves [rope, map, key].

question: removeIf is given a test. What does this print?
feedback: The arrow reads "given an element d, is d % 2 == 0?", which is true for even numbers. removeIf deletes every element that passes the test, so 6, 4 and 2 go. The survivors keep their original order: [3, 1, 5]. Nothing is sorted, and the test describes what to REMOVE, not what to keep.

incorrect: names.add(s + "!");
names.remove(s);
names.add(0, s);
feedback: The loop objects to STRUCTURAL changes, the ones that alter how many elements the list has: every form of add and remove. set replaces one element and leaves the size alone, so it is allowed, and size() and indexOf only read. (remove can occasionally slip through without an exception, when it happens on the second-to-last pass, but the loop then silently skips an element. It is a bug either way.)

question: An ArrayList keeps its elements side by side in an array. A LinkedList keeps each element in its own node, holding links to the node before and the node after. With many thousands of elements, which of these claims are true?
correct: add(0, x), inserting at the very front, is much quicker on the LinkedList
get(i) for an i near the middle is much quicker on the ArrayList
incorrect: add(i, x) for an i near the middle is much quicker on the LinkedList, since no elements have to shift
The LinkedList needs less memory per element, since it has no spare array slots
A LinkedList cannot be stored in a variable of type List, as it has no array inside
A for-each loop over the LinkedList fails, since its elements have no index
feedback: An ArrayList can jump straight to slot i, but inserting at the front makes it shift every element along. A LinkedList adds at either END by relinking a node or two, which is why it is quick there. The middle is the famous trap: nothing shifts, true, but a LinkedList has to WALK node by node to reach position i first, and that walk is far slower than the ArrayList's shift. Measured, middle inserts are tens of times slower on the LinkedList. Each node also carries two links, so it uses more memory, not less. Both classes are Lists, and both work in a for-each loop.

question: Match each collection to the job it suits best.

pairs.definition: A leaderboard that changes often and is read by position: 1st, 2nd, 3rd
The usernames already taken, checked at every sign-up, no repeats
Each player's name, used to look up that player's gold
A waiting line: players join at the back and leave from the front
The seven day names, which no code should be able to alter

feedback: Ask what the program does most. Reading by position and changing over time: ArrayList. "Have I seen this before?" with no duplicates: HashSet. Looking one thing up by another: HashMap. Working only at the two ends: LinkedList (ArrayDeque is the other common choice for a queue). Data that must never change: List.of, which refuses every add, set and remove.

incorrect: nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(7));
nums.indexOf(7);
feedback: fixed came from List.of, so it is immutable and set throws UnsupportedOperationException. nums has indexes 0 to 2. get(3) is out of range. remove(3) has an int argument, so it means position 3, not the value 3, and that is out of range too. add(5, 0) tries to insert at position 5 of a 3-element list: inserting is allowed at positions 0 to 3, no further. All three throw IndexOutOfBoundsException. Looking for a value that is not there is not an error: remove(Object) just returns false, and indexOf returns -1.

question: words is a String[] of creature names. Arrange these lines into a fragment that counts how often each name appears and then prints the count for "elf".
feedback: The map has to exist before the loop can use it. The put line belongs INSIDE the loop, because it is the only place w exists, and it must run once per word. The println comes after the closing brace, once every word has been counted; placed inside, it would print a running count on every pass.

feedback_template: The first loop builds [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]: the value at index i is i * 10. Each remove(0) deletes the front element and every other element slides one index to the left. After {{r}} removals, the element now at index {{k}} is the one that started {{r}} places further right, and its value is {{expected}}.

question: Three kinds of collection work together here. What does this print?
feedback: Copying rolls into a HashSet drops the duplicates, leaving 2, 4 and 6 in no promised order. A Set cannot be sorted, so the values are copied into an ArrayList, and reverseOrder() makes it [6, 4, 2]. best.remove(1) has an int argument, so it deletes POSITION 1 (the 4), not the value 1. rolls is a List.of list that nothing here tried to change: still 5 elements.
